subject: Chemistry
title: Equilibrium
summary: This chapter builds the idea of a dynamic balance between forward and reverse processes — physical equilibria first, then chemical equilibrium, equilibrium constants, Le Chatelier's principle, and finally ionic equilibrium in acids, bases, buffers and salts.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 has no board exam, but this is one of the longest and most heavily tested chapters in the school final, and it is the direct foundation for Class 12 Electrochemistry, Chemical Kinetics and the whole of Physical Chemistry numericals in JEE and NEET. Ionic equilibrium (pH, Ka, Kb, buffers, Ksp) is tested every single year in competitive exams.

question_types.note: Direction of Kc/Kp shift, units of K, conjugate acid-base pairs, pH of a given concentration, common ion effect, Le Chatelier predictions.
Whether adding a catalyst/inert gas/pure solid changes K or equilibrium position; relation between Kp and Kc; buffer action.
Write Kc expression for a given reaction; state Le Chatelier's principle; define pH, buffer, common ion effect.
Effect of pressure/temperature/concentration change on a given equilibrium; a Kc–Kp numerical; pH of a weak acid/base.
Full ICE-table numerical for Kc or degree of dissociation; Henderson–Hasselbalch buffer calculation; solubility product problem with common ion effect.
A passage on a real equilibrium system (Haber process, blood buffer, antacid) with 4 sub-questions mixing concept and calculation.

hot_topics: Law of mass action, Kc and Kp, and the relation Kp = Kc(RT)Δn
Le Chatelier's principle applied to concentration, pressure, temperature and catalyst changes
ICE table numericals — finding K or equilibrium concentrations
Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis acid-base concepts and conjugate pairs
pH, pOH and Ka/Kb calculations for weak acids and bases, including Ostwald's dilution law
Buffer solutions and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
Common ion effect and solubility product (Ksp)
Factors affecting equilibrium and characteristics of equilibrium state

sections.heading: 6.1 Equilibrium in Physical Processes
sections.body:
Equilibrium is a state where two opposing processes occur at the same rate, so there is no further net change even though both processes keep happening — this is why it is called dynamic, not static. NCERT builds the idea through three physical examples before moving to chemical reactions.

Solid–liquid: H2O(s) ⇌ H2O(l). At the melting point (0 °C, 1 atm) the rate of melting equals the rate of freezing; the mass of ice and water in an insulated vessel stays constant with time, though molecules keep crossing the interface both ways.

Liquid–vapour: H2O(l) ⇌ H2O(g). In a closed vessel, evaporation and condensation reach a stage where the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation; the pressure exerted by the vapour at this point is the vapour pressure of the liquid at that temperature, and it depends only on temperature, not on the amount of liquid present.

Solid–vapour (sublimation): solid ⇌ vapour, e.g. camphor, iodine, ammonium chloride subliming in a closed container — a saturated vapour pressure is again reached.

Solute–solution (solubility equilibrium): when a saturated solution is in contact with undissolved solute, the rate of dissolution equals the rate of crystallisation, e.g. sugar(s) ⇌ sugar(solution). Solubility of a solid in a liquid is fixed at a given temperature at saturation.

Gas–solution (Henry's law): for a gas dissolving in a liquid under pressure, e.g. soda water, the equilibrium concentration of dissolved gas is proportional to the pressure of the gas above the liquid — this is Henry's law, and it explains why a sealed cold-drink bottle fizzes on opening (pressure drop shifts CO2 equilibrium toward the gas phase).
sections.tip: General characteristics common to all physical equilibria: equilibrium is possible only in a closed system, both opposing processes occur simultaneously, they occur at equal rates at equilibrium, and all measurable properties (mass, pressure, concentration, colour) become constant with time — an examiner favourite one-mark fill-in.

sections.heading: 6.2 Equilibrium in Chemical Processes — Dynamic Equilibrium
sections.body:
A chemical reaction is said to reach equilibrium when the rate of the forward reaction becomes exactly equal to the rate of the reverse reaction, so the concentrations of reactants and products no longer change with time — again dynamic, not static, because both reactions continue at the molecular level. Chemical equilibrium can be approached from either direction: starting with only reactants, or only products, or a mixture — the same equilibrium state (same Kc at a given temperature) is reached, which is a direct consequence of the law of mass action.

NCERT's classic illustration is the reaction of H2 and I2 to form HI in a closed vessel at constant temperature: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Whether the vessel is charged with H2 + I2, or with pure HI, or with a mixture of all three, the system settles to the same ratio of concentrations at equilibrium at that temperature — this is experimentally how the reversibility and equilibrium nature of the reaction was established.

Chemical equilibria are classified as homogeneous (all species in the same phase, e.g. the HI system above, or N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)) and heterogeneous (species in more than one phase, e.g. CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g)).
sections.tip: A reaction that appears to have 'stopped' (no visible change) is not necessarily complete — check whether both reactants and products are still present, which is the signature of equilibrium rather than completion.

sections.heading: 6.3 Law of Chemical Equilibrium and Equilibrium Constant
sections.body:
For a general reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at a given temperature, the law of chemical equilibrium (law of mass action, given by Guldberg and Waage) states that at equilibrium the ratio of the product of equilibrium concentrations of the products (each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient) to the product of equilibrium concentrations of the reactants (each raised to its coefficient) is a constant, called the equilibrium constant Kc.

Kc = [C]c[D]d / [A]a[B]b, where square brackets denote equilibrium molar concentrations.

Key facts examiners test: (i) Kc has a fixed value at a given temperature and changes only with temperature, never with initial concentrations or the presence of a catalyst; (ii) pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the Kc expression because their 'concentration' (density/molar mass) is constant and gets absorbed into K, e.g. for CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), Kc = [CO2]; (iii) the value of K depends on how the equation is written — if an equation is reversed, K is inverted (K′ = 1/K); if an equation is multiplied by a factor n, K is raised to the power n (K′ = Kn); if two equations are added, the resultant K is the product of the two K values; (iv) a very large Kc (≫103) means the reaction proceeds nearly to completion (products favoured); a very small Kc (≪10−3) means the reaction barely proceeds (reactants favoured); a Kc close to 1 (10−3 to 103) means appreciable amounts of both are present at equilibrium.

where: equilibrium constant in terms of molar concentration
equilibrium molar concentration of species X

sections.tip: If asked to reverse or scale a reaction and find the new K, never add or subtract K values directly — apply the inversion/power rule, then multiply if combining equations.

sections.heading: 6.4 Homogeneous Equilibria — Relation between Kp and Kc
sections.body:
For gas-phase reactions it is often more convenient to express the equilibrium constant in terms of partial pressures, Kp, since partial pressure is proportional to concentration (from PV = nRT, P = (n/V)RT = cRT). For the general reaction aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g), Kp is related to Kc by:

Kp = Kc(RT)Δn, where Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants) = (c + d) − (a + b).

Special cases students must know: if Δn = 0, Kp = Kc (e.g. H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)); if Δn > 0, Kp > Kc; if Δn < 0, Kp < Kc. R must be in units consistent with P and V — commonly R = 0.0831 L bar K−1 mol−1 when pressure is in bar (NCERT's SI convention) and T in kelvin.

NCERT worked example type: for N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), Δn = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)−2, i.e. Kp = Kc / (RT)2.

where: equilibrium constant in terms of partial pressure
moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants
0.0831 L bar K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> (or 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)

sections.tip: Always double-check whether the question wants R in L atm or L bar units — using the wrong R with the wrong pressure unit is the single most common numerical slip in this topic.

sections.heading: 6.5 Heterogeneous Equilibria
sections.body:
An equilibrium in a system with more than one phase is heterogeneous. The equilibrium constant expression omits pure solids and pure liquids since their activity (effectively their concentration) stays constant. Standard NCERT examples: CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), Kc = [CO2], Kp = PCO2; Ag2O(s) + 2HNO3(aq) ⇌ 2AgNO3(aq) + H2O(l), Kc = [AgNO3]2/[HNO3]2 (water and Ag2O omitted).

An important consequence: for CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), Kc depends only on temperature — so at a fixed temperature the equilibrium pressure of CO2 above CaCO3/CaO is fixed and does not depend on how much CaCO3 or CaO is present, only on whether both solid phases are present.
sections.tip: Common trap: students write concentration terms for solids/liquids out of habit. Only gases and species in aqueous solution appear in K; pure solids and pure liquids never do.

sections.heading: 6.6 Applications of Equilibrium Constant
sections.body:
Three standard uses of K, all frequently asked as short-answer questions:

(a) Predicting the extent of a reaction — as noted above, K ≫ 1 means the reaction goes nearly to completion, K ≪ 1 means it barely proceeds, and K close to unity means comparable amounts of reactants and products coexist.

(b) Predicting the direction of a reaction (reaction quotient Qc) — Qc has the same expression as Kc but uses concentrations at any point in time, not necessarily at equilibrium. Comparing Qc to Kc tells which way the reaction will shift to reach equilibrium: if Qc < Kc, the reaction proceeds forward (net formation of more products, since not enough product is present yet); if Qc > Kc, the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction; if Qc = Kc, the reaction is already at equilibrium.

(c) Calculating equilibrium concentrations — using an ICE (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) table: write initial concentrations, express the change in terms of an unknown x (or the degree of dissociation α) using the stoichiometric ratios, add to get equilibrium concentrations, then substitute into the Kc expression and solve for x. This is the standard method for every numerical in this chapter, ionic equilibrium included.

formulas.expr: Qc = [C]<sup>c</sup>[D]<sup>d</sup> / [A]<sup>a</sup>[B]<sup>b</sup> (at any instant, not necessarily equilibrium)

sections.tip: Whenever a question gives 'some concentrations at a point in time' and asks for the direction of the reaction, compute Qc and compare with the given Kc — do not just eyeball it.

sections.heading: 6.7 Factors Affecting Equilibria — Le Chatelier's Principle
sections.body:
Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure, volume or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to counteract (partially undo) the effect of that change.

Effect of concentration: adding more reactant (or removing product) shifts equilibrium forward; adding more product (or removing reactant) shifts it backward. Example: in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, adding N2 or H2, or removing NH3 as it forms, drives the equilibrium toward more NH3 — the industrial basis of the Haber process.

Effect of pressure/volume: increasing pressure (decreasing volume) shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas; decreasing pressure shifts it toward the side with more moles of gas. If Δn = 0 (equal moles both sides), pressure change has no effect on the position of equilibrium. Example: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (4 mol → 2 mol) is favoured by high pressure.

Effect of temperature: this is the one factor that also changes the value of K itself, not just the position of equilibrium. For an exothermic reaction (ΔH negative), increasing temperature shifts equilibrium backward (K decreases); for an endothermic reaction (ΔH positive), increasing temperature shifts equilibrium forward (K increases). Example: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol−1 (exothermic) — industrially run at a moderate ~700 K compromise (rate vs yield), not at low temperature despite low T favouring yield.

Effect of a catalyst: a catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally. It has no effect on the position of equilibrium or on the value of K — it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster.

Effect of adding an inert gas: at constant volume, adding an inert gas does not change the partial pressures of the reacting species, so equilibrium is undisturbed. At constant pressure, adding an inert gas increases the total volume, which lowers the partial pressures of reacting gases — the equilibrium then shifts toward the side with more moles of gas (same effect as decreasing pressure).
sections.tip: The 'inert gas at constant volume vs constant pressure' distinction is a very common Assertion-Reason and MCQ trap — read the question carefully for which condition (V or P) is held fixed.

sections.heading: 6.8 Optimising the Conditions for Industrial Processes
sections.body:
NCERT gives two applied case studies that combine Le Chatelier's principle with real industrial conditions — both are common in case-based questions.

Haber process for ammonia: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol−1. High pressure (~200 atm) favours the forward reaction (fewer moles on product side); low temperature would favour yield (exothermic), but industrially a moderate temperature (~700 K) is used with an iron catalyst (with Mo promoter) to get a workable reaction rate, since too low a temperature makes the reaction too slow to be economical. Removing NH3 as it liquefies also drives the equilibrium forward continuously.

Contact process for sulphuric acid: the key step 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) is also exothermic; excess O2 (from air) and a moderate temperature (~720 K) with a V2O5 catalyst are used for a similar rate-vs-yield compromise.
sections.tip: For any industrial-process question, first identify whether ΔH is negative or positive, then state the pressure/temperature choice as a trade-off between equilibrium yield and rate — examiners reward mentioning both.

sections.heading: 6.9 Ionic Equilibrium in Solution — Acids, Bases and Electrolytes
sections.body:
Substances that conduct electricity in molten or aqueous state are electrolytes; strong electrolytes (HCl, NaOH, NaCl) ionise almost completely, weak electrolytes (CH3COOH, NH4OH) ionise only partially and set up an ionic equilibrium between unionised molecules and ions.

Arrhenius concept: an acid furnishes H+ ions and a base furnishes OH− ions in aqueous solution. Limitation: applies only to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basicity of substances like NH3 that have no OH−.

Bronsted-Lowry concept: an acid is a proton (H+) donor, a base is a proton acceptor. Every acid, on losing a proton, forms its conjugate base, and every base, on accepting a proton, forms its conjugate acid — together an acid and the base formed from it (or vice versa) are called a conjugate acid-base pair, e.g. HCl (acid) / Cl− (conjugate base); NH3 (base) / NH4+ (conjugate acid). A species that can act as both, like H2O or HCO3−, is amphoteric. The conjugate base of a strong acid is always weak, and the conjugate acid of a strong base is always weak (inverse strength relationship within a pair).

Lewis concept: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor, a base is an electron-pair donor — this is the broadest definition and explains acidic behaviour of species with no H at all, e.g. BF3, AlCl3 (Lewis acids, electron-deficient) and NH3, H2O (Lewis bases, lone pair donors).
sections.tip: A favourite MCQ: identify the conjugate acid-base pair in a given reaction, or identify which species is amphiprotic (can donate or accept a proton) — H<sub>2</sub>O, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> are the standard examples.

sections.heading: 6.10 Ionisation of Water, pH and the Ionic Product of Water
sections.body:
Water undergoes self-ionisation (autoprotolysis): H2O + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH−, often written simply as H2O ⇌ H+ + OH−. The equilibrium constant for this, called the ionic product of water (Kw), is Kw = [H+][OH−], and at 25 °C, Kw = 1.0 × 10−14. Kw increases with temperature (ionisation is endothermic), so pure water becomes slightly more acidic-seeming (lower pH) at higher T while remaining neutral ([H+] = [OH−]).

Sørensen's pH scale: pH = −log10[H+] (strictly [H3O+]). At 25 °C: neutral solution has pH = 7 ([H+] = [OH−] = 10−7 M); acidic solution has pH < 7; basic solution has pH > 7. Similarly pOH = −log10[OH−], and since Kw = [H+][OH−] = 10−14, taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C (an examiner-favourite one-liner, valid only at 25 °C).

For strong acids/bases (assumed to dissociate completely), [H+] or [OH−] is taken directly from the given concentration times the number of ionisable H/OH per formula unit, e.g. for 0.01 M HCl, [H+] = 0.01 M, pH = 2; for 0.01 M Ca(OH)2, [OH−] = 0.02 M.
sections.tip: pH + pOH = 14 holds only at 25 °C — if a question gives Kw at a different temperature, recompute using pH + pOH = −log<sub>10</sub>Kw, do not blindly use 14.

sections.heading: 6.11 Ionisation Constants of Weak Acids and Bases (Ka, Kb) and Ostwald's Dilution Law
sections.body:
For a weak acid HA ⇌ H+ + A−, the acid ionisation constant Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA]. A larger Ka means a stronger acid. Similarly for a weak base BOH ⇌ B+ + OH−, Kb = [B+][OH−]/[BOH].

Degree of ionisation (α) is the fraction of the total number of moles that ionises at equilibrium. For a weak acid of initial concentration c, using an ICE table (initial c, 0, 0; change −cα, +cα, +cα; equilibrium c(1−α), cα, cα): Ka = (cα)(cα) / c(1−α) = cα2/(1−α). When α is small (weak acid, α ≪ 1), 1 − α ≈ 1, giving Ostwald's dilution law: Ka ≈ cα2, so α ≈ √(Ka/c) — the degree of ionisation increases as the solution is diluted (c decreases). Then [H+] = cα = √(Ka·c), and pH = ½(pKa − log c).

pKa and pKb: pKa = −log10Ka, pKb = −log10Kb. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid. For a conjugate acid-base pair, Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = 14 (at 25 °C) — this lets pKb of a conjugate base be found directly from the pKa of the acid, and vice versa.

Relative strength of two acids at the same concentration can be compared using α1/α2 = √(Ka1/Ka2), derived directly from Ostwald's law.

formulas.expr: Ka = cα<sup>2</sup>/(1−α) ≈ cα<sup>2</sup> for α ≪ 1 (Ostwald's dilution law)
where: initial molar concentration of the weak acid

formulas.expr: Ka × Kb = Kw; pKa + pKb = 14 (at 25 °C, for a conjugate acid-base pair)
where: base ionisation constant of the conjugate base

sections.tip: Never assume 1 − α ≈ 1 for a strong or moderately ionising acid (α not small) — solve the full quadratic cα<sup>2</sup> + Kaα − Ka = 0 in that case; the approximation is valid only when Ka/c is small (roughly α < 0.05).

sections.heading: 6.12 Common Ion Effect on the Ionisation of Acids and Bases
sections.body:
The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte that furnishes an ion common to the weak electrolyte's equilibrium. Example: adding CH3COONa (fully ionised) to a solution of CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO− + H+ increases [CH3COO−], and by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts backward (left), reducing the ionisation of the weak acid and lowering [H+] — this is exactly the mechanism used to prepare a buffer solution.

Similarly, adding NH4Cl to NH4OH suppresses the ionisation of the weak base by supplying a common NH4+ ion. Common ion effect is also central to controlling precipitation, e.g. adding H2S in the presence of dilute HCl (common H+) in qualitative salt analysis selectively precipitates only very insoluble sulphides.
sections.tip: Common ion effect and Le Chatelier's principle are the same idea applied to ionic equilibrium — always answer 'why' using the shift-away-from-added-species logic, not just naming the effect.

sections.heading: 6.13 Hydrolysis of Salts and the pH of Salt Solutions
sections.body:
Salts formed from the reaction of an acid and a base can be classified by the strength of their parent acid/base, and their aqueous solutions are not always neutral because the ions can react with water (hydrolysis).

Salt of strong acid + strong base (e.g. NaCl): neither ion hydrolyses, solution is neutral, pH = 7.

Salt of strong acid + weak base (e.g. NH4Cl): the cation hydrolyses (NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH4OH + H+), releasing H+, so the solution is acidic, pH < 7.

Salt of weak acid + strong base (e.g. CH3COONa): the anion hydrolyses (CH3COO− + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH−), releasing OH−, so the solution is basic, pH > 7.

Salt of weak acid + weak base (e.g. CH3COONH4): both ions hydrolyse; the resulting pH depends on the relative strengths (Ka vs Kb) of the parent acid and base — solution is close to neutral if Ka ≈ Kb, acidic if Ka > Kb, basic if Kb > Ka.
sections.tip: A very common short-answer question gives four salts and asks which is acidic/basic/neutral — answer by naming the parent acid and base strength for each, not just stating the conclusion.

sections.heading: 6.14 Buffer Solutions and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation
sections.body:
A buffer solution resists a change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or base, or on dilution. An acidic buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base (e.g. CH3COOH + CH3COONa); a basic buffer is a mixture of a weak base and its salt with a strong acid (e.g. NH4OH + NH4Cl).

How it works (mechanism): in an acidic buffer, the large reservoir of CH3COO− (from the fully ionised salt) neutralises any added H+ by combining with it to form unionised CH3COOH, while the large reservoir of unionised CH3COOH neutralises any added OH− by releasing H+ to replace it (via the equilibrium) — either addition is absorbed by shifting a large existing equilibrium only slightly, so pH barely changes.

The pH of a buffer is given by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, derived from the Ka expression of the weak acid: Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA], so [H+] = Ka × [HA]/[A−]; taking −log of both sides, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]). For a basic buffer, pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]).

Buffers are important physiologically — blood is maintained at pH ≈ 7.4 by the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer (H2CO3/HCO3−).

where: concentration of the conjugate base (e.g. CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>)
concentration of the undissociated weak acid

sections.tip: A buffer works best (maximum buffering capacity) when [salt] = [acid], i.e. when pH = pKa — this is a frequent one-mark conceptual question.

sections.heading: 6.15 Solubility Equilibrium of Sparingly Soluble Salts — Solubility Product (Ksp)
sections.body:
For a sparingly soluble salt in a saturated solution, e.g. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq), the equilibrium constant is called the solubility product, Ksp = [Ag+][Cl−] (the pure solid is omitted, as usual for heterogeneous equilibria). For a general salt AxBy(s) ⇌ xAy+ + yBx−, Ksp = [Ay+]x[Bx−]y.

If solubility (moles dissolved per litre) is S, for a 1:1 salt like AgCl, [Ag+] = [Cl−] = S, so Ksp = S2, S = √Ksp. For a salt like Ag2CrO4 (Ag2CrO4 ⇌ 2Ag+ + CrO42−), [Ag+] = 2S, [CrO42−] = S, so Ksp = (2S)2(S) = 4S3.

Predicting precipitation using the ionic product (Qsp): if the ionic product Qsp (calculated from given/mixed concentrations, same expression as Ksp) is greater than Ksp, the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs; if Qsp = Ksp, the solution is exactly saturated (equilibrium, no net change); if Qsp < Ksp, the solution is unsaturated and no precipitation occurs (or existing precipitate would dissolve).

Common ion effect on solubility: adding a common ion (e.g. NaCl to a saturated AgCl solution) increases [Cl−], and since Ksp is fixed at a given temperature, [Ag+] must decrease — i.e. the solubility of AgCl decreases in the presence of a common ion. This is used to purify salts by 'salting out'.
sections.tip: For salts with different ion ratios (1:1 vs 1:2 vs 2:3), the relation between Ksp and S is different every time — always write the dissociation equation and set up [ion] in terms of S from scratch rather than recalling a memorised formula.

key_terms.definition: A state where the forward and reverse processes occur continuously at equal rates, so measurable properties of the system stay constant with time.
The constant ratio of the product of equilibrium concentrations of products to that of reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, at a given temperature.
The same expression as Kc but evaluated at any point during the reaction (not necessarily at equilibrium); comparing Qc with Kc predicts the direction the reaction will shift.
If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure, volume or temperature, the equilibrium shifts to partially counteract that change.
A chemical equilibrium in which all reactants and products are in the same phase, e.g. all gases.
A chemical equilibrium in which reactants and products are present in more than one phase; pure solids and liquids are excluded from the equilibrium constant expression.
An acid is a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) donor and a base is a proton acceptor; the species formed after donation/acceptance is its conjugate base/acid.
A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor; this concept explains acidic behaviour even without a transferable proton.
Kw = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>], equal to 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C; it increases with temperature.
The negative logarithm to base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration, pH = −log<sub>10</sub>[H<sup>+</sup>]; used to express acidity/basicity on a convenient scale.
The fraction of the total number of moles of a weak electrolyte that has ionised at equilibrium.
For a weak electrolyte, Ka ≈ cα<sup>2</sup> when α is small, so the degree of ionisation increases on dilution (α ∝ 1/√c).
The suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte caused by adding a strong electrolyte that supplies an ion common to the weak electrolyte's equilibrium.
A solution (weak acid + its salt, or weak base + its salt) that resists a change in pH on adding small amounts of acid, base, or on dilution.
The reaction of the cation or anion of a dissolved salt with water, producing H<sup>+</sup> or OH<sup>−</sup> and making the salt solution acidic or basic rather than neutral.
The equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble salt, equal to the product of the molar concentrations of its ions, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

Below the table write Ka = x<sup>2</sup>/(c−x) and show the simplification to cα<sup>2</sup> when x ≪ c, connecting directly to Ostwald's dilution law.

diagrams.title: Henderson–Hasselbalch buffer action
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a beaker containing a large pool of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> ions and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH molecules (roughly equal numbers). Draw one H<sup>+</sup> ion being added from a dropper with an arrow into the beaker, then an arrow showing it combining with a CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> to form CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (pool of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> shrinks slightly, pool of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH grows slightly). Caption: 'large reservoirs absorb the added H<sup>+</sup>, so pH changes only slightly'.

ncert_questions.q: A liquid is in equilibrium with its vapour in a sealed container at a fixed temperature. The volume of the container is suddenly increased. (a) What is the initial effect of the change on vapour pressure? (b) How do the rates of evaporation and condensation change initially? (c) What happens when equilibrium is restored finally and what will be the final vapour pressure?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The vapour now occupies a larger space, so vapour pressure decreases initially.

(b) Rate of evaporation stays roughly the same (depends on liquid surface and T, not volume); rate of condensation decreases, since the more dilute vapour gives fewer collisions with the surface. So evaporation > condensation, and net evaporation occurs.

(c) More liquid evaporates until the rates are equal again. Since T is unchanged, the final vapour pressure equals the original value — vapour pressure depends only on temperature, not volume.

ncert_questions.q: What is Kc for the reaction: 2NOCl(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), given equilibrium concentrations [NOCl] = 0.06 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, [NO] = 0.02 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, [Cl<sub>2</sub>] = 0.01 mol L<sup>−1</sup>?

At a certain temperature and total pressure of 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, iodine vapour contains 40% I atoms by mole fraction. Kp for I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2I(g) is (assume Kp is 3.76 in appropriate units). Calculate Kp for the equilibrium and comment on the extent of dissociation. (Simplified NCERT-style working shown for the standard version of this question.)
ncert_questions.a:
P = 105 Pa. Mole fraction I = 0.4, I2 = 0.6, so PI = 0.4×105 Pa, PI2 = 0.6×105 Pa.

Kp = (PI)2/PI2 = (0.4×105)2/(0.6×105) = 1.6×109/0.6×105 ≈ 2.67 × 104 Pa — a fairly large value, so I2 dissociates quite extensively at this temperature.

ncert_questions.q: Write the conjugate acids for the following Bronsted bases: NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, NH<sub>3</sub>, and HCOO<sup>−</sup>.
ncert_questions.a: A conjugate acid is formed by adding one H+ to the base. NH2− + H+ → NH3 (conjugate acid: NH3). NH3 + H+ → NH4+ (conjugate acid: NH4+). HCOO− + H+ → HCOOH (conjugate acid: HCOOH).

ncert_questions.q: Write the conjugate bases for the following Bronsted acids: HF, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>.
ncert_questions.a: A conjugate base is formed by removing one H+ from the acid. HF − H+ → F− (conjugate base: F−). H2SO4 − H+ → HSO4− (conjugate base: HSO4−). HCO3− − H+ → CO32− (conjugate base: CO32−).

ncert_questions.q: The concentration of hydrogen ion in a sample of soft drink is 3.8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M. What is its pH?
ncert_questions.a:
pH = −log10[H+] = −log10(3.8 × 10−3) = −(log 3.8 + log 10−3) = −(0.5798 − 3) = 3 − 0.5798 = 2.42.

So the pH of the soft drink is about 2.42 (acidic, as expected for a carbonated drink).

ncert_questions.q: The ionisation constant of HF is 3.2 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Calculate the degree of dissociation of HF in its 0.02 M solution. Calculate the concentration of all species present (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, F<sup>−</sup> and HF) in the solution.
ncert_questions.a:
Ka = cα2/(1−α), Ka = 3.2×10−4, c = 0.02 M. Ka/c is not tiny, so solve the quadratic cα2 + Kaα − Ka = 0, i.e. 0.02α2 + 3.2×10−4α − 3.2×10−4 = 0. By the quadratic formula, α ≈ 0.119 (11.9%).

[H3O+] = [F−] = cα ≈ 2.38 × 10−3 M; [HF] remaining = c(1−α) ≈ 1.76 × 10−2 M.

ncert_questions.q: The pH of a 0.1 M monobasic acid is 4.50. Calculate the concentration of the species H<sup>+</sup>, A<sup>−</sup> and HA at equilibrium. Also determine the value of Ka and pKa of the monobasic acid.
ncert_questions.a:
[H+] = 10−pH = 10−4.50 = 3.16 × 10−5 M. Since HA ⇌ H+ + A−, [A−] = [H+] = 3.16 × 10−5 M. [HA] at equilibrium = 0.1 − 3.16×10−5 ≈ 0.1 M (negligible change since ionisation is very small).

Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA] = (3.16×10−5)2 / 0.1 = 1.0 × 10−9 / 0.1 = 1.0 × 10−8. pKa = −log(1.0 × 10−8) = 8.0.

ncert_questions.q: The ionisation constant of nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) is 4.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Calculate the pH of 0.04 M sodium nitrite solution and also determine the degree of hydrolysis of NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>.
ncert_questions.a:
NO2− hydrolyses: NO2− + H2O ⇌ HNO2 + OH−. Kb = Kw/Ka = 10−14/4.5×10−4 = 2.22 × 10−11.

h = √(Kb/c) = √(2.22×10−11/0.04) ≈ 2.36 × 10−5. [OH−] = ch ≈ 9.43 × 10−7 M, pOH ≈ 6.03, pH = 14 − 6.03 = 7.97.

ncert_questions.q: A 0.02 M solution of pyridinium hydrochloride has pH = 3.44. Calculate the ionisation constant of pyridine (given the conjugate relationship pyridinium ion/pyridine).
ncert_questions.a:
Pyridinium ion (C5H5NH+) is the conjugate acid of pyridine, and it hydrolyses/ionises as a weak acid: C5H5NH+ ⇌ C5H5N + H+. [H+] = 10−3.44 ≈ 3.63 × 10−4 M.

Ka(pyridinium) = [H+]2/c = (3.63×10−4)2 / 0.02 = 1.32×10−7/0.02 = 6.6 × 10−6. Kb(pyridine) = Kw/Ka = 1.0×10−14 / 6.6×10−6 ≈ 1.52 × 10−9.

ncert_questions.q: The solubility product of Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> is 2.7 × 10<sup>−11</sup>. Calculate its molar solubility.
ncert_questions.a:
Al(OH)3(s) ⇌ Al3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq). Let solubility = S; [Al3+] = S, [OH−] = 3S. Ksp = [Al3+][OH−]3 = S(3S)3 = 27S4.

27S4 = 2.7 × 10−11, so S4 = 1.0 × 10−12, S = (1.0 × 10−12)1/4 ≈ 1.0 × 10−3 mol L−1.

ncert_questions.q: Equal volumes of 0.002 M solutions of sodium iodate (NaIO<sub>3</sub>) and cupric chlorate (Cu(ClO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) are mixed. Will a precipitate of Cu(IO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> form? Ksp for Cu(IO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> at room temperature is 7.4 × 10<sup>−8</sup>.
ncert_questions.a:
On mixing equal volumes, each concentration is halved: [IO3−] = 0.001 M, [Cu2+] = 0.001 M.

Qsp = [Cu2+][IO3−]2 = (0.001)(0.001)2 = 1.0 × 10−9.

Since Qsp (1.0 × 10−9) < Ksp (7.4 × 10−8), the solution is unsaturated with respect to Cu(IO3)2, so no precipitate forms.

ncert_questions.q: Explain why pure liquids and solids are not included in the equilibrium constant expression, using CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) as an example.
ncert_questions.a: The concentration (mol/volume) of a pure solid or pure liquid equals its density divided by its molar mass, both of which are constant at a given temperature — the 'concentration' does not change no matter how much of the solid/liquid is present, so it is not a variable and gets merged into the constant K itself rather than appearing explicitly. For CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), only CO2 is a gas with a variable concentration, so Kc = [CO2] and Kp = PCO2 — both CaCO3 and CaO are left out.

ncert_questions.q: A buffer solution contains equal concentrations of a weak acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) and its sodium salt. Calculate the pH.
ncert_questions.a:
Using Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). Since [salt] = [acid], log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

pKa = −log(1.8 × 10−5) = −(log 1.8 − 5) = −(0.2553 − 5) = 4.745.

So pH ≈ 4.74.

pyq.q: For the reaction N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g), the units of Kc are:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Kc = [NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2</sup>/([N<sub>2</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3</sup>); Δn(mol basis) for the denominator power sum is 4 in denom vs 2 in numerator, giving units of (mol/L)<sup>2−4</sup> = (mol/L)<sup>−2</sup> = mol<sup>−2</sup>L<sup>2</sup>.

pyq.q: Which of the following changes will NOT alter the value of the equilibrium constant Kc of a reaction?
options: Changing the pressure at constant temperature (for a reaction with Δn ≠ 0)
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Kc depends only on temperature. A catalyst changes only the rate at which equilibrium is reached, and a pressure/volume change at constant temperature shifts the position of equilibrium but never the value of K itself.

pyq.q: The conjugate base of HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Removing one H<sup>+</sup> from HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> gives SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, its conjugate base.

pyq.q: On dilution, the degree of ionisation (α) of a weak acid:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: By Ostwald's dilution law, α ≈ √(Ka/c); as c decreases on dilution, α increases.

pyq.q: For the equilibrium 2SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>(g), ΔH = −ve, an increase in temperature will:
options: Increase Kc and shift equilibrium forward
Decrease Kc and shift equilibrium backward
Have no effect on Kc but shift equilibrium forward
Increase Kc but shift equilibrium backward
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The forward reaction is exothermic; raising temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction by Le Chatelier's principle, and since the reaction is exothermic in the forward direction, Kc decreases with increasing temperature.

pyq.q: The pH of a 10<sup>−8</sup> M HCl solution is closest to:
options: 6.98 (slightly acidic, close to 7, considering water's own ionisation)
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: At such a low concentration, the contribution of water's autoionisation ([H<sup>+</sup>] from water ≈ 10<sup>−7</sup>) cannot be ignored; the actual [H<sup>+</sup>] works out to slightly above 10<sup>−7</sup> M, giving a pH just under 7 (about 6.98), not 8 — a classic trap testing whether students blindly apply pH = −log(c).

pyq.q: Which of the following is an example of a Lewis acid but not a Bronsted-Lowry acid?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: BF<sub>3</sub> is electron-deficient and accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid) but has no proton to donate, so it cannot be a Bronsted-Lowry acid.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Addition of an inert gas at constant volume to a system at equilibrium does not disturb the equilibrium. Reason (R): At constant volume, adding an inert gas does not change the partial pressures or concentrations of the reacting species.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both statements are true, and R correctly explains why equilibrium is undisturbed at constant volume — the partial pressures of the reacting gases stay exactly as they were.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of a reversible reaction. Reason (R): A catalyst increases the rate of both the forward and the reverse reaction equally.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: A catalyst does NOT change the equilibrium yield (A is false) — it only helps the system reach the same equilibrium faster, because it speeds up both directions equally (R is true).

pyq.q: Assertion (A): pKa + pKb = 14 for any acid and any base. Reason (R): Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate acid-base pair at 25 °C.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: R is true, but A is stated too broadly — the relation pKa + pKb = 14 holds only for a conjugate acid-base pair (the acid and the base derived from it), not for any arbitrary unrelated acid and base.

pyq.q: Write the expression for Kc for the reaction: 4NH<sub>3</sub>(g) + 5O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 4NO(g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O(g).
pyq.answer: Kc = [NO]<sup>4</sup>[H<sub>2</sub>O]<sup>6</sup> / [NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>4</sup>[O<sub>2</sub>]<sup>5</sup>. All four species are gases, so all appear with their stoichiometric coefficients as powers.

pyq.q: State Le Chatelier's principle. Predict the effect of increasing pressure on: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
pyq.answer: Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure, temperature or volume, the equilibrium shifts in a direction that tends to counteract the effect of that change. For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so a change in pressure has no effect on the position of this equilibrium.

pyq.q: Define buffer solution. Give one example each of an acidic and a basic buffer.
pyq.answer: A buffer solution resists a change in its pH on the addition of small amounts of an acid or a base, or on dilution. Acidic buffer example: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + CH<sub>3</sub>COONa (mixture of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base). Basic buffer example: NH<sub>4</sub>OH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (mixture of a weak base and its salt with a strong acid).

pyq.q: What is the common ion effect? Give one example.
pyq.answer: The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte on adding a strong electrolyte that furnishes an ion common to the weak electrolyte's equilibrium. Example: adding CH<sub>3</sub>COONa to CH<sub>3</sub>COOH solution increases [CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>], which by Le Chatelier's principle shifts CH<sub>3</sub>COOH ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> backward, suppressing further ionisation of the acid.

pyq.q: For the reaction 2A(g) ⇌ 2B(g) + C(g), the value of Kc at 500 K is 0.30. At a particular time, [A] = 0.02 M, [B] = 0.03 M and [C] = 0.06 M. Predict the direction in which the reaction will proceed to reach equilibrium.
pyq.answer:
Qc = [B]2[C]/[A]2 = (0.03)2(0.06) / (0.02)2 = (9×10−4)(0.06) / (4×10−4) = 5.4×10−5/4×10−4 = 0.135.
Since Qc (0.135) < Kc (0.30), the reaction has not yet reached equilibrium and there is proportionally too little product — the reaction will proceed in the forward direction (more B and C will form) until Qc rises to equal 0.30.

pyq.q: Explain, with a reason, whether the pH of a 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COONa solution is expected to be greater than, less than, or equal to 7.
pyq.answer: CH<sub>3</sub>COONa is the salt of a weak acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) and a strong base (NaOH). The acetate ion hydrolyses: CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + OH<sup>−</sup>. This releases OH<sup>−</sup> ions into solution, making [OH<sup>−</sup>] > [H<sup>+</sup>], so the solution is basic — its pH is greater than 7. (The sodium ion, being the conjugate of a strong base, does not hydrolyse.)

pyq.q: Kc for the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g) is 4.9 × 10<sup>−3</sup> at 350 K. If a system contains A, B and C each at 1.0 M concentration initially, what will be the direction of the reaction?
pyq.answer:
Qc = [B][C]/[A] = (1.0)(1.0)/(1.0) = 1.0.
Since Qc (1.0) > Kc (4.9 × 10−3), there is too much product relative to reactant compared with equilibrium — the reaction will proceed in the reverse direction, converting some B and C back to A, until Qc falls to 4.9 × 10−3.

pyq.q: For the reaction PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ⇌ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), write the relation between Kp and Kc and calculate Δn.
pyq.answer:
Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants) = (1 + 1) − 1 = 1.
Kp = Kc(RT)Δn = Kc(RT)1 = Kc·RT (using R and T with consistent units for pressure, e.g. R = 0.0831 L bar K−1 mol−1 if pressure is in bar).

pyq.q: 13.8 g of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> was placed in a 1 L closed vessel at a certain temperature and allowed to reach equilibrium: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2NO<sub>2</sub>(g). At equilibrium, 50% of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> was dissociated. Calculate the equilibrium constant Kc for this reaction. (Molar mass of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 92 g/mol)
pyq.answer:
Initial moles of N2O4 = 13.8/92 = 0.15 mol; in a 1 L vessel, initial [N2O4] = 0.15 M.

ICE table for N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g):
Initial: [N2O4] = 0.15, [NO2] = 0
Change: −0.15×0.5 = −0.075, +2(0.075) = +0.15
Equilibrium: [N2O4] = 0.15 − 0.075 = 0.075 M, [NO2] = 0.15 M

Kc = [NO2]2/[N2O4] = (0.15)2/0.075 = 0.0225/0.075 = 0.30 mol L−1.

pyq.q: Derive the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer from first principles (starting from the Ka expression). Then calculate the pH of a buffer made by mixing 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COONa (Ka of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>).
pyq.answer:
Derivation: For HA ⇌ H+ + A−, Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA]. With the salt fully ionised and common-ion suppression of HA, [HA] ≈ [acid] and [A−] ≈ [salt], so [H+] = Ka·[acid]/[salt]. Taking −log of both sides: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).

Calculation: pKa = −log(1.8×10−5) = 4.745. Since [salt] = [acid], log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.74.

pyq.q: The solubility of CaF<sub>2</sub> in water is 2.05 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> at 25 °C. Calculate its Ksp. Also calculate the solubility of CaF<sub>2</sub> in a 0.01 M NaF solution (common ion effect), stating the simplifying assumption used.
pyq.answer:
CaF2(s) ⇌ Ca2+ + 2F−. With S = 2.05×10−4 M, [Ca2+] = S, [F−] = 2S, so Ksp = 4S3 = 4(2.05×10−4)3 ≈ 3.45 × 10−11.

In 0.01 M NaF, [F−] ≈ 0.01 M (F− from CaF2 is negligible next to this). Let new solubility = S′ = [Ca2+]: Ksp = S′(0.01)2 = 3.45×10−11, so S′ = 3.45 × 10−7 mol L−1 — far lower than in pure water, confirming the common ion effect suppresses solubility.

pyq.q: Explain, using Le Chatelier's principle, why the Haber process for ammonia synthesis is industrially carried out at a moderately high temperature (~700 K) and high pressure (~200 atm) with an iron catalyst, even though the forward reaction is exothermic and low temperature would favour a higher equilibrium yield.
pyq.answer:
N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol−1. Low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield (Le Chatelier), but the forward rate would then be too slow to be commercial, so a moderate ~700 K is chosen as a rate-yield compromise.

Δn = 2 − 4 = −2, so high pressure (~200 atm) shifts equilibrium toward the fewer-mole product side, raising NH3 yield and rate together. The iron catalyst (with Mo promoter) speeds up reaching equilibrium without changing its position or Kc. Removing NH3 by liquefaction as it forms keeps pulling the equilibrium forward.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
Human blood is maintained at a pH of about 7.35–7.45 by the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer system: H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. Metabolic processes constantly add acidic (CO2, lactic acid) or occasionally basic substances to the blood, yet the pH barely shifts because of this buffer. The ratio [HCO3−]/[H2CO3] in normal blood is about 20:1, and pKa of carbonic acid (H2CO3) in blood is about 6.1.
(i) Name the type of buffer this is (acidic or basic) and identify the acid and its salt/conjugate base in this system.
(ii) Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and the given data, calculate the pH of blood predicted by this ratio.
(iii) If lactic acid is added to the blood during intense exercise, explain, using Le Chatelier's principle, how this buffer resists a large drop in pH.
(iv) Why does the buffer stop working effectively if a very large amount of acid is added at once?
pyq.answer:
(i) An acidic buffer — the weak acid is H2CO3, its conjugate base/salt is HCO3−.

(ii) pH = pKa + log([HCO3−]/[H2CO3]) = 6.1 + log 20 = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.40, matching normal blood pH.

(iii) Added H+ combines with the large HCO3− reservoir (H+ + HCO3− → H2CO3). Since the reservoir is large relative to the added H+, the ratio [HCO3−]/[H2CO3] changes only slightly, so pH changes only slightly.

(iv) The buffer's capacity is limited by how much HCO3− reservoir exists. A very large acid dose consumes it all, leaving nothing to neutralise further H+, so the buffer is exhausted and pH then drops rapidly.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
In the industrial synthesis of methanol, the reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) ⇌ CH3OH(g) is exothermic (ΔH < 0) and is carried out at high pressure over a catalyst. A chemical engineer studies how changing conditions affects the equilibrium yield of methanol.
(i) Calculate Δn for this reaction and predict the effect of increasing pressure on the equilibrium yield of methanol.
(ii) Predict, with reason, the effect of increasing temperature on the equilibrium yield.
(iii) The engineer adds a catalyst to speed up the process. Will this change the equilibrium yield of methanol? Justify.
(iv) If pure CO and H2 gas (no methanol) are sealed in a rigid vessel and allowed to reach equilibrium, will the same equilibrium composition be obtained as starting from pure methanol vapour under identical conditions? Explain.
pyq.answer:
(i) Δn = 1 − (1+2) = −2. Fewer gas moles on the product side, so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium forward, raising methanol yield.

(ii) The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising temperature shifts equilibrium in the reverse direction (Le Chatelier), decreasing yield, though it raises the rate of reaching equilibrium.

(iii) No — a catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally; it changes neither Kc nor the equilibrium yield.

(iv) Yes, the same equilibrium composition results either way, because equilibrium at a given temperature is fixed by Kc and stoichiometry, not by the starting point — a defining feature of chemical equilibrium.

practice_mcq.q: At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction is:
options: Equal to the rate of the reverse reaction
Greater than the rate of the reverse reaction
Less than the rate of the reverse reaction
practice_mcq.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic — both reactions continue but at equal rates, so no net change is observed.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these is a heterogeneous equilibrium?
practice_mcq.explanation: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) involves species in two phases (solid and gas), making it heterogeneous; the other three are all-gas, homogeneous equilibria.

practice_mcq.q: For a reaction, if Kc = 10<sup>10</sup>, the reaction:
options: Proceeds to a very small extent
Is at equilibrium with equal reactant and product concentrations
practice_mcq.explanation: A very large Kc (≫ 10<sup>3</sup>) indicates the equilibrium lies far to the product side — the reaction goes nearly to completion.

practice_mcq.q: If Δn = 0 for a gaseous reaction, then:
options: Kp and Kc cannot be compared
practice_mcq.explanation: Kp = Kc(RT)<sup>Δn</sup>; when Δn = 0, (RT)<sup>0</sup> = 1, so Kp = Kc.

practice_mcq.q: Increasing pressure on the equilibrium 2SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>(g) will:
practice_mcq.explanation: Δn = 2 − 3 = −1; the product side has fewer gas moles, so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward SO<sub>3</sub> (forward).

practice_mcq.q: The strength of a Bronsted acid is measured by its tendency to:
practice_mcq.explanation: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is defined as a proton donor; a stronger acid donates protons more readily (higher Ka).

practice_mcq.q: Which pair represents a conjugate acid-base pair?
practice_mcq.explanation: H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> is formed by adding H<sup>+</sup> to H<sub>2</sub>O, so H<sub>2</sub>O/H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> is a conjugate base/acid pair.

practice_mcq.q: The ionic product of water at 25 °C is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Kw = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C, a standard value to memorise.

practice_mcq.q: As temperature increases, Kw of water:
practice_mcq.explanation: The self-ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw increases with temperature (pure water becomes 'more ionised', pH drops slightly, but it stays neutral).

practice_mcq.q: A solution has pH = 5. Its hydrogen ion concentration is:
Which salt solution is expected to be acidic?
practice_mcq.explanation: NH<sub>4</sub>Cl is the salt of a weak base (NH<sub>4</sub>OH) and a strong acid (HCl); the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion hydrolyses to release H<sup>+</sup>, making the solution acidic.

practice_mcq.q: A buffer solution has maximum buffering capacity when:
practice_mcq.explanation: When [salt] = [acid], pH = pKa exactly, and the buffer has equal reserves to neutralise either added acid or added base — this is the point of maximum buffering capacity.

practice_mcq.q: Adding NaCl to a saturated solution of AgCl (in equilibrium with solid AgCl) will:
options: Dissolve all the solid AgCl instantly
practice_mcq.explanation: This is the common ion effect: added Cl<sup>−</sup> increases [Cl<sup>−</sup>], and since Ksp = [Ag<sup>+</sup>][Cl<sup>−</sup>] is fixed, [Ag<sup>+</sup>] (and hence solubility) must decrease.

practice_mcq.q: For A<sub>2</sub>B<sub>3</sub> type salt with molar solubility S, the solubility product Ksp is:
Which of the following acts as a Lewis base?
practice_mcq.explanation: NH<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair on nitrogen that it can donate to an electron-deficient species, making it a Lewis base; BF<sub>3</sub>, AlCl<sub>3</sub> and H<sup>+</sup> are electron-pair acceptors (Lewis acids).

practice_mcq.q: In the reaction CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, water acts as a:
practice_mcq.explanation: Water accepts a proton from CH<sub>3</sub>COOH to form H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, so it acts as a proton acceptor — a Bronsted base — in this reaction.

practice_mcq.q: A reaction has Qc < Kc at a given instant. The reaction will:
options: Remain exactly as it is, at equilibrium already
practice_mcq.explanation: Qc < Kc means there is proportionally less product than at equilibrium, so the reaction proceeds forward to increase products until Qc rises to equal Kc.

common_mistakes: Writing concentration terms for pure solids or pure liquids in the Kc/Kp expression — they must be omitted entirely, not written as 1.
Confusing the effect of a catalyst: students often think it shifts equilibrium or changes K, when it only changes how fast equilibrium is reached.
Using the approximation 1 − α ≈ 1 (Ostwald's dilution law) even when Ka/c is not small, giving a wrong degree of ionisation — the full quadratic must be solved when the approximation is not valid.
Mixing up R units (L atm vs L bar) when converting between Kp and Kc, or forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin.
Assuming pH + pOH = 14 always holds, forgetting this is true only at 25 °C when Kw = 10<sup>−14</sup>.
Not distinguishing Qc from Kc — comparing given concentrations directly to K without computing Qc first, and drawing the wrong conclusion about the direction of the reaction.
Forgetting that adding an inert gas at constant pressure (not constant volume) does shift the equilibrium, because it changes the total volume and hence the partial pressures.
Writing the solubility product formula for A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>y</sub> type salts incorrectly by not raising each ion concentration to its own stoichiometric power.
strategy:
This is a long chapter with two clearly separable halves — general chemical equilibrium (Sections 6.1–6.8) and ionic equilibrium (6.9–6.15) — and both are tested every year, so don't skip either half. Start by mastering the Kc/Kp expressions and the ICE-table method: almost every numerical, in both halves of the chapter, is really the same ICE-table technique applied to a different equilibrium (dissociation, ionisation, hydrolysis, or solubility). Practise writing the Kc expression for a random reaction without looking anything up until it is automatic, remembering to drop pure solids and liquids.

Memorise cold: Kw = 10−14 at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14 (at 25 °C only), the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, and the general Ksp-solubility relation for 1:1, 1:2 and 2:3 type salts. Le Chatelier's principle questions are conceptual and high-yield for the time they take — be ready to apply it separately to concentration, pressure/volume, temperature, catalyst and inert-gas changes, since exams often ask about more than one factor for the same reaction in a single question.

For long-answer numericals, always set up the ICE table explicitly rather than jumping to a memorised shortcut formula — the marking scheme rewards showing initial, change and equilibrium rows. Keep the Haber process and Contact process case studies ready as worked examples of Le Chatelier's principle in an industrial setting, since case-based questions frequently draw on them.
revision_checklist: Can state the characteristics common to all physical equilibria (closed system, opposing processes, equal rates, constant measurable properties).
Can write the Kc expression for any given reaction, correctly omitting pure solids and liquids.
Knows the relation Kp = Kc(RT)<sup>Δn</sup> and can compute Δn correctly.
Can distinguish homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria with an example of each.
Understands how Qc predicts the direction of a reaction relative to Kc.
Can state Le Chatelier's principle and apply it separately to concentration, pressure, temperature, catalyst and inert gas.
Can explain the rate-vs-yield compromise in the Haber process and Contact process.
Can distinguish Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis acid-base definitions and identify conjugate acid-base pairs.
Knows Kw = 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C and that pH + pOH = 14 only at 25 °C.
Can set up and solve an ICE table for a weak acid/base ionisation, including Ostwald's dilution law and its approximation limits.
Can explain the common ion effect and predict its direction using Le Chatelier's principle.
Can classify a salt (from strong/weak acid + strong/weak base) and predict whether its solution is acidic, basic or neutral.
Can derive and apply the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for buffer pH.
Can write the Ksp expression for any A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>y</sub> salt and relate it to molar solubility S.
Can compare Qsp with Ksp to predict whether a precipitate will form.
